prompt.brief: Design a multi-region disaster-recovery architecture that meets explicit RPO/RTO targets, replicates data and artifacts, detects regional failure, fails over safely, and supports tested restoration and failback.
successSignals: Classify data by replication and recovery requirements, define the write authority, and document RPO, RTO, and acceptable data loss.
Automate infrastructure and configuration from versioned definitions while fencing an old primary to prevent split-brain writes.
Replicate databases, objects, secrets, queues, and observability evidence with independent lag and integrity checks.
Explain health detection, DNS or global routing, degraded mode, restore drills, failback, operator approval, and auditability.

functional: Provision a secondary region, replicate state and artifacts, monitor lag, declare an incident, fail over, and restore traffic.
Expose regional health, replication lag, RPO estimate, failover readiness, data validation, and recovery progress.
Support automatic detection with controlled promotion, operator override, backup restore, failback, and recovery drills.
nonFunctional: Meet RPO below five minutes and a documented RTO for each workload class; do not claim zero loss without synchronous replication.
Replicate thousands of resources and high-volume data streams without one control-plane queue becoming a failover bottleneck.
Make failover, promotion, restore, and client retries idempotent and fence stale writers before serving the new region.
Serve degraded read-only or cached functionality while replication or a dependent region is unavailable.
scaleAssumptions: Protect 100 services across three regions, with databases, objects, queues, secrets, and infrastructure definitions.
Partition replication and recovery by service, tenant, data class, and region; isolate high-write workloads.
Retain backups, replication manifests, restore logs, failover decisions, and drill evidence under retention policy.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Multi-region disaster-recovery architecture latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
